'''St. Augustine grass'''  (''Stenotaphrum secundatum''), also known as '''buffalo turf''' in Australia and '''buffalo grass''' in South Africa, is a species of grass in the family [[Poaceae]]. It is a warm-season [[lawn grass]] that is popular for cultivation in [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] regions. It is a medium- to high-maintenance grass that forms a thick, carpetlike [[sod]], crowding out most [[weed]]s and other grasses.

==Characteristics ==
[[File:St. Augustine grass with St. Augustine Decline infection.jpg|thumb|right|Specimens with the [[Panicum mosaic virus|St. Augustine decline]] infection]]
St. Augustine is a dark green grass with broad, flat blades. It spreads by aboveground [[stolon]]s, commonly known as "runners", and forms a dense layer.

The grass occurs on both sides of the [[Atlantic Ocean]],<ref name="hear">{{cite web | url = http://www.hear.org/pier/species/stenotaphrum_secundatum.htm | title = ''Stenotaphrum secundatum'' (Walter) Kuntze | work = Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER) }}</ref> including much of the southeastern United States, Texas,<ref>{{cite web | url = http://aquat1.ifas.ufl.edu/node/439 | title = St. Augustine grass | publisher = Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090122102843/http://aquat1.ifas.ufl.edu/node/439 | archive-date = 2009-01-22 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Stenotaphrum secundatum'' (Walter) Kuntze |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/plant-profile/STSE |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170708103403/https://plants.usda.gov/core/profile?symbol=STSE |archive-date=2017-07-08 |access-date=2026-07-06 |work=USDA PLANTS}}</ref> Mexico, and Central and South America.<ref name="hear" /> It has escaped cultivation in [[California]],<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=7783 | title = Taxon Report 7783: ''Stenotaphrum secundatum'' | work = The CalFlora Database }}</ref> Hawaii, many Pacific islands, [[South Africa]] and [[New Zealand]].<ref name="hear"/><ref>[https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/51763 Stenotaphrum secundatum (buffalo grass)<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

St. Augustine grass occurs in most [[Caribbean]] and [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean]] areas. It grows best in tropical climates. It is often seen in [[lagoon]]s and [[marsh]]es, on shorelines, and wherever there is a good amount of moisture.

==Planting and propagation==
Only recently has commercially valuable and viable seed for St. Augustine become available, so it has typically been propagated by [[Plug (horticulture)|plug]]s, [[sprigging|sprig]]s, or sod. Once the grass is [[Agriculture|cultivate]]d, it can propagate on its own.

St. Augustine can grow in a wide range of soil types with a [[pH]] between 5.0 and 8.5. It usually blooms in spring and summer.

==Uses==
St. Augustine grass is commonly used in pastures and on ranches. It is a popular lawn grass, rivalling [[bermudagrass]], though St. Augustine is somewhat less [[drought]]-tolerant.

==Cultivars==
A number of [[cultivar]]s have been developed:<ref name=tren>Trenholm, L. E., et al. [http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/lh010 St. Augustinegrass for Florida Lawns.] Publication #ENH5. University of Florida IFAS. 1991. Revised 2011.</ref>
*'Captiva' - released in 2007. Developed by the [[University of Florida]] for its resistance to the [[Blissus insularis|southern chinch bug]]<ref name=buss>Buss, E. A. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/242460000_Southern_Chinch_Bug_Management_on_St_Augustinegrass_1 "Southern Chinch Bug Management on St. Augustinegrass".] Publication #ENY-325. University of Florida IFAS. 1993. Revised 2010.</ref> and its dwarf profile, which requires less [[mowing]].
*'Floratam' - released in 1973. Developed during an academic collaboration between the University of Florida and [[Texas A&M University]].<ref>[http://today.tamu.edu/2012/09/06/collaboration-between-texas-am-and-university-of-florida-creates-popular-lawn-grass/ Collaboration Between Texas A&M And University Of Florida Creates Popular Lawn Grass - Texas A&M Today<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Resists the viral infection [[Panicum mosaic virus|St. Augustine decline]] (SAD). Not as cold- or shade-tolerant.
*'Floratine' - released in 1959. Has a darker color and finer texture. Tolerates lower temperatures and needs less mowing.
*'Palmetto' - released in the mid-1990s. A smaller, lighter green grass.
*'Raleigh' - released in 1980. Tolerant of cold, but susceptible to insects and disease.
*'Sapphire' - released in 2004. Selected from Australia for its dark blue-green leaves and purple stolons and rapid lateral growth.
*'Seville' - released in 1980. Similar to 'Floratam', but with a finer [[Surface texture|texture]].
*'Sir Walter Buffalo' - released in 1996. Developed for Australian conditions with traits such as heat and drought.<ref>{{cite web |title=History of Sir Walter Buffalo Lawn |url=https://grechsturf.com.au/history-of-sir-walter/ |website=Grech's Turf Supplies |access-date=6 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414154323/https://grechsturf.com.au/history-of-sir-walter/ |archive-date=14 April 2021}}</ref>
*'Texas Common' - Most similar to the natural species, it has fallen out of favor due to its susceptibility to the incurable St. Augustine decline virus.
*'Variegatum' - in 1993  it is given the prestigious [[Award of Garden Merit]] by the Royal Horticulture Society. It is a creeping evergreen grass with striped white leaves.
